handTraceIndependentlyPerformed.finding: Part A's fix wraps ONLY the console.error call in its own try/catch. It never re-examines its own premise that classifyError is total. classifyError is NOT total: `String(err)` on a non-Error value invokes the value's own `toString`/`Symbol.toPrimitive`, and `err.message` on an actual Error instance invokes that instance's own `message` accessor - both are user-controlled and can throw. Both call sites (line 427 and line 484) sit OUTSIDE any try/catch, unlike the console.error call Part A fixed. A JS `catch` block cannot catch an exception raised from within itself (or from a nested try/catch after it has already propagated past that nested block); such an exception propagates directly out of the enclosing function, uncaught.

assessmentOfPartAsClaim.whatPartAGotRight: The console.error tertiary tier genuinely is now wrapped in its own try/catch and genuinely cannot throw uncaught by itself - re-confirmed by construction 5 here and unchanged from Part A's own construction 3. The failureRecordPersisted/failureRecordError/failureRecordFallbackLogged result-contract fields are real and correctly populated whenever the function reaches its `return` statement.
assessmentOfPartAsClaim.wherePartAsClaimOverreaches: Part A's hand-trace (08-failure-observability-bottom.json, `handTracedConfirmationNoCodePathCanThrowUncaught`) asserts classifyError 'cannot throw for any JS value' and is therefore 'canThrow: false' at both its call sites, WITHOUT itself wrapping either call site in a try/catch. That assertion is empirically false for realistic adversarial inputs (a non-Error value with a throwing toString/Symbol.toPrimitive, or an Error instance with a throwing message getter) - both of which are unremarkable in a codebase that ultimately interacts with a driver (Prisma) and third-party/wrapped values, not merely hand-authored plain Errors. Because both classifyError call sites sit outside any try/catch (unlike the console.error call Part A did fix), the SAME class of defect OPEN-6 was opened to close - an uncaught escape from runContractAnalysis's own failure-recording path, with no FAILED result, no console trace, and no durable row - still reproduces today, one or two statements earlier than the location Part A patched.

dispositionRationale: OPEN-6 is NOT closed. Part A's fix correctly hardened the console.error tertiary fallback but did not hold up the same standard against its own load-bearing helper, classifyError, at either of its two unguarded call sites (orchestrator.ts:427 and orchestrator.ts:484). Four independent, freshly-authored adversarial constructions (a non-Error thrown value with a throwing toString at the original-failure site, the same shape at the recording-failure site, an Error instance with a throwing .message getter, and a synchronous-throw variant) each reproduce an exception propagating uncaught out of runContractAnalysis, with no FAILED result returned, no console trace emitted, and no AnalysisFailureLog row written - the exact 'log-only/no-visibility failure mode' this whole workstream exists to eliminate. A fifth construction (circular-reference payload reaching console.error's own argument) did NOT reproduce an escape and is reported as a non-finding for completeness. Recommended remediation (not applied, per this task's read-only-on-production-code constraint): wrap each of the two classifyError(...) call sites in orchestrator.ts (lines 427 and 484) in its own try/catch with a total, hand-verified fallback (e.g. a hardcoded classification such as { message: "<unclassifiable error>", errorClass: "UnknownError" } on any failure to classify), matching the same standard already applied to the console.error call.
